headline: He walked 31,000 miles home. It took 28 years.
summary: Karl Bushby left his mother's house in Hull, England, in 1998 to walk around the world. On Monday he walked back in. He set out from Punta Arenas, Chile, crossed four continents and 30 countries, walked the Bering Strait ice and swam the English Channel rather than take a boat. He is 57. His mother asked, "Where have you been?"

cover_question.q: Did he walk across the ocean?

cover_answer: No. He swam the Channel and walked the Bering Strait ice.
table_question: What promise would you keep for 28 years?

5-7.script: A man named Karl walked all the way around the world and got home to his mum on Monday. He left when he was 29 and he is 57 now, and he walked 31,000 miles, more than once around the whole Earth. When the sea was in the way he swam, or walked over the ice. His mum had a banner up that said "Welcome Home Son."
5-7.why: One man, one walk, one mum at the gate. The miles become a lap of the Earth so they can picture it.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script gives them one picture: a man walking, and a mum at the gate with a banner. The miles mean nothing until they become a lap of the Earth. Expect "did he miss his mum?" Yes. He hadn't seen her in ten years, and she cried.

8-12.script: Karl Bushby made himself one rule in 1998: every mile home on foot, like a board game where you can't skip a square. That rule is why it took 28 years: Bering Strait ice, a decade of Russian visa trouble and a crash that took his sponsors' money. On Monday he walked into Hull.
8-12.why: A rule they could have written, and the chain of what it cost. The board game is a game they have played.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and what they cost, so the script hands them the rule first, feet only, and then the chain it set off: ice, visas, money, 28 years. A board game square they can't skip is a rule they have argued over. Expect "why didn't he cheat once?" Because then it wouldn't be the walk.

13-17.script: Would you give 28 years to one promise? Karl Bushby said in 1998 he would walk every mile home or not come home, and on Monday, at 57, he did. He barely saw his son grow up. Second: he says it took a world of strangers to get him there. Whose win is it?
13-17.why: Two true things: the promise kept, and the years it took from other people. Let them weigh it.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once, and this story is two: a promise kept to the mile, and a son who grew up without him. The script hands them both, then flips it with his own line that the win belongs to the strangers. Expect "would you have done it?" Answer honestly. The point is the argument.

5-7.q: Did he walk across the ocean?
5-7.a: No. He swam the English Channel and walked across the Bering Strait when it was frozen. He wouldn't get on a boat or a plane.

8-12.a: Feet only was the rule. Frozen seas, visas and money stopped him.
An American, Dimitry Kieffer, crossed the Bering Strait ice with him.

13-17.a: He doesn't know what's next. He's 57, moving into his mum's basement.
His dad's birthday card asked if a man could walk London to New York.
